name: Drospirenone

lead: Drospirenone is a prescription progestin related to spironolactone. In the combined pill Yaz it is labelled for moderate acne in women at least 14 who also choose the pill for contraception.
Its antiandrogenic and antimineralocorticoid actions are the usual explanation for the acne benefit and for less fluid retention than some older progestins.

paras: It activates the progesterone receptor to suppress ovulation while blocking androgen and mineralocorticoid receptors, which lowers androgen signalling in skin.

Common effects include headache, irregular bleeding, nausea, breast tenderness and mood changes. Combined pills carry a boxed warning for smokers over 35, and registry studies have reported more venous clots with drospirenone pills than with levonorgestrel pills, though the size of the difference is debated. Rarely it can raise potassium. Prescription-only.

lead: Drospirenone is a synthetic progestin structurally related to the diuretic spironolactone. In addition to activating the progesterone receptor, it blocks the mineralocorticoid and androgen receptors, which gives it a profile that is often described as closer to natural progesterone than that of older progestins.[1][2] It is taken by mouth, most often combined with an estrogen in contraceptive pills, and also as a progestogen-only pill.[1]

For appearance purposes its relevance is acne. A US-labelled combination of drospirenone and ethinyl estradiol (Yaz) is indicated to treat moderate acne in women at least 14 years old who also want an oral contraceptive, alongside its contraceptive and premenstrual dysphoric disorder indications.[3] Its antiandrogenic activity is the mechanism usually cited for this effect.[1][2]

Drospirenone pills carry the same boxed warning about smoking and cardiovascular events as other combined oral contraceptives, and large registry studies and a network meta-analysis have examined whether drospirenone-containing pills are associated with more venous thromboembolism than levonorgestrel pills.[3][4][5][6]

paras: Drospirenone combined with ethinyl estradiol has an FDA-labelled indication for moderate acne in women aged 14 and over who choose an oral contraceptive for birth control.[3] Grokipedia attributes the acne benefit to drospirenone's antiandrogenic activity, and Wikipedia lists acne, premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder among indications for the low-dose ethinylestradiol pills.[1][2]
The acne indication is tied to use as a contraceptive: the label limits it to patients who desire contraception, so it is not an acne-only treatment.

Drospirenone is used for contraception in combined pills (with ethinyl estradiol or estetrol) and in a progestogen-only pill (Slynd, approved in the US in 2019), and for menopausal hormone therapy together with estradiol (Angeliq).[1] It has also been used as a component of hormone therapy for transgender women.[1]

The US label for drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol reports headache or migraine, menstrual irregularities, nausea or vomiting, breast pain and mood changes as the most frequent adverse reactions in contraception and acne trials.[3] Wikipedia also lists weight gain and acne among reported effects and notes that hyperkalemia is rare but that potassium monitoring is advised in higher-risk patients, such as those with kidney disease or on potassium-raising drugs, because of drospirenone's antimineralocorticoid action.[1]

The label carries a boxed warning that cigarette smoking raises the risk of serious cardiovascular events with combined oral contraceptives, particularly in women over 35, and states that such women should not use the product.[3]

Combined pills containing ethinyl estradiol raise the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) compared with non-use. Whether drospirenone differs from older progestins has been examined in several studies. The Danish national cohorts and the Dutch MEGA case-control study reported higher VTE rates with drospirenone-containing pills than with levonorgestrel pills, while a network meta-analysis compared many pill types.[4][5][6][7] The FDA label states that drospirenone combined pills may be associated with a higher VTE risk than levonorgestrel-containing ones and advises weighing this before starting them.[3]

A large European active surveillance study of a drospirenone-containing pill covering 142,475 woman-years reported its own safety findings.[8] Wikipedia notes the relative-risk estimates (roughly 1.3 to 2.0 times levonorgestrel in some studies) are debated because of possible confounding, and that Bayer has faced litigation over clots, with many cases settled.[1] Danish data have also examined stroke and myocardial infarction with hormonal contraception.[9]

Drospirenone acts as an agonist of the progesterone receptor and an antagonist of the androgen and mineralocorticoid receptors, without estrogenic activity; it suppresses ovulation.[1][3][10] Its antimineralocorticoid action counters sodium and water retention that estrogens can promote, which is why it is described as less likely to cause bloating-type effects than some other progestins.[1][11] Reviews of progestin pharmacology classify it among agents with antiandrogenic properties.[12]

Per Wikipedia, oral bioavailability is roughly 66 to 85 percent, protein binding about 95 to 97 percent and elimination half-life about 25 to 33 hours, with metabolism largely independent of cytochrome P450 enzymes though CYP3A4 inhibitors can raise levels.[1] A 2000 review characterised its pharmacokinetics in detail.[10]

Drospirenone was synthesised and patented in 1976 by Schering AG, including chemist Rudolf Wiechert, as a spironolactone-derived progestin.[2] It was first marketed in 2000 in a pill with ethinylestradiol (Yasmin in Europe), and the US FDA approved Yasmin in 2001; Yaz, a lower-dose 24/4 regimen, followed in 2006.[1][2] A progestogen-only pill was approved in 2019 and an estetrol combination in 2021.[1]

Brand names include Yasmin, Yaz, Slynd (Slinda in some regions), Nextstellis and Angeliq; generics are widely available.[1] It is prescription-only in the US, Canada and Australia.[1] Litigation over blood clots in users of Bayer's drospirenone pills has been reported.[1] No community discussion sources were reviewed for this entry.

Efficacy for contraception has been studied in large trials, for example a 13-cycle Phase 3 study of a 4.0 mg drospirenone-only pill in about 1,550 participants.[13] Registered current trials include drospirenone-only pill pharmacokinetics after bariatric surgery, estetrol/drospirenone in endometriomas, and use of drospirenone in adenomyosis.[14][15][16] Acne is addressed in the approved labelling for the ethinyl estradiol combination, which reports it was studied in contraception and acne clinical trials.[3] Safety has been examined in the cohort and case-control studies described above.[4][5][6][8]
